title: Fix mode and re-review rules
bridge: A Byte fix PR is like a teammate's PR into your feature branch. You merge it, and your PR to main is reviewed as usual. Except the person who asked for the fix is now part of the change. So main needs its approval from someone else, on the head that contains the fix.
intro: After its first review, Byte does two more things. When a developer asks, it fixes its own findings (fix mode). On each new push it runs a cheap check, the sniff, to see whether its findings are fixed. This lesson makes fix mode safe on main and lets fcp skip full re-reviews when the sniff is sure.

picture.caption: A fix carries the requester's name into main; the checks re-run on the new head; someone else approves.

p: Someone comments @byte-fix on a PR in fcp. Byte's .github/workflows/fix.yml starts scripts/fix-driver.sh. A plan session decides what to change, and an act session changes it. Then checks run with no network, with one repair round if they fail.

The result is a PR from a branch named byte/fix-<pr>-<sha> into the author's branch, never into main. Some paths are never edited: the protected list FIX_FLOOR in src/fix-paths.ts. The author reviews the fix PR and merges it into their branch.
No CI runs on the fix PR itself. Security signed off fix mode on that basis: SECURITY.md lists it as residual 3. A residual is a known risk that Security accepted, with a number in that file.

Picture Dana's PR to main. Omer is reviewing it and comments @byte-fix on two findings. Byte writes the fix, Dana merges it into her branch, and Omer approves the PR. Omer asked for that code, and then approved it.

Today the rule against this is a team habit. SECURITY.md writes it as residual 1: a developer other than the requester reviews each fcp fix PR. Nothing enforces it. Fix PRs merge into feature branches, which have no ruleset, so main is the only place GitHub can enforce it.
G2-05 turns the habit into a check. Byte writes who asked into every fix commit, and G0's independent-approval check on main reads it.

callout.text: The requester never approves their own agent's work. For a Byte fix, the requester is whoever commented @byte-fix, even if they are only a reviewer of the PR.

p: A trailer is a Key: value line at the end of a commit message, after a blank line. Git can read it back by key, so a check can ask for the Requested-by of every commit without parsing prose.

SECURITY.md keeps model text out of commit messages, and that rule stays. The trailer is not model text: it is the login Byte's gate already checked when it accepted the @byte-fix command. The function still refuses anything that is not a GitHub login.
sections.because: We put the requester in the commit itself, because the fix commit is what reaches main, where the check reads it.

notes.text: The comment says why this trailer is allowed despite the no-model-text rule. Update the old 'No trailers' comment to match.
A GitHub login: 1 to 39 letters, digits or hyphens. Nothing else can reach the commit message.
Refuse anything else. A login that fails here is a bug in the gate, not something to clean up.
The trailer line itself. No @ in the commit; the PR body line has one.
The existing function gains a requester field. Its other inputs are unchanged.
Today's lines stay exactly as they are: finding ids and plain-path locations.
An empty line separates the message body from the trailers. Git needs it to find them.
The trailer goes last, so git log reads it as a trailer.
The PR body keeps its prose and adds the machine line, the same one the orchestrator writes for Nova.

sections.h: The check on main reads the trailers
p: G0-09's check already builds a requester set and counts approvals on the head commit. G2-05 extends it for fcp main PRs. It finds the commits made by Byte's fix identity, reads their Requested-by trailers, and adds those logins to the set.

It also asks that the approval is newer than the last fix commit. An approval given before the fix was merged cannot have seen the fix. The sketch below is built from the ticket's steps; the fix identity's exact login comes from Nave.
sections.because: We fail closed on a fix commit without a trailer, because a missing name would let anyone, including the requester, approve.

notes.text: The trailer pattern, with an optional @ so the body line and the commit line both match.
Only the commit fields we need: who made it, its message and when.
Input: the PR's commits and the login Byte's fix commits are made by.
Keep only the fix commits. Commits by people are handled by G0-09's commit-author rule.

callout.text: The G2-05 ticket never names the login that Byte's fix commits are made by. fixIdentity is that login, and the check is useless with a wrong one. Ask Nave for the exact login before you write the check, and put it in a test.

p: The second rule of G2-05 is green required checks on the head that contains the fix. It needs no new workflow. Merging the fix into the branch changes the PR's head, so G0's required checks run again. The ruleset's dismiss stale approvals setting drops any approval given before.

Do not add a pull_request workflow that runs on fix PRs. Security's sign-off, residual 3, relies on none running there. Instead, say it plainly in the fix PR banner and the result comment. The ticket's sentence: 'CI runs when you merge this into your branch; main then needs green checks and an approval from someone other than @<requester>.'

The merge rate of fix PRs already exists in src/fix-fates.ts and on Byte's dashboard. The G1 nightly metrics job reads data/fix-fates.jsonl from the telemetry branch and writes byte_fix_prs_total{state} for Grafana.

callout.text: Update SECURITY.md residuals 1 and 5 in the same PR, and ask Security to re-confirm the fix-mode sign-off. A wall that changed needs its paperwork to change too.

p: On every push after the first review, Byte runs the sniff. It is a cheap model call on TypeSafe's Jev model. For each open Byte finding it answers: did this push fix it? Each answer is fulfilled or not, with a confidence.

A sniff is sure when its confidence is at least fulfilConfidence, 0.85 for fcp. When every open finding is fulfilled and sure, live mode posts a short sniff line instead of a full re-review. That saves a full review on a push that only fixed findings.

fcp runs the sniff in observe mode. The sniff runs and records its answer, but the full review runs anyway. So every sniff in fcp has a paired full review to check it against. The pairs live in data/sniffs.jsonl and data/sniff-pairs.jsonl on Byte's telemetry branch, shown on the dashboard's sniff page.

sections.h: Two bars and the Wilson bound
p: A false fulfilled is a sniff that was fulfilled and sure, while the paired full review flagged the finding again. In live mode that push would have skipped a review it needed. The bar is at most 2%. The skip rate is the share of all-fixed pushes the sniff would skip. It must be at least 40%, or going live saves too little.

A small sample can look perfect by luck. Zero false out of 60 looks like 0%, but the true rate could still be 6%. The Wilson upper bound is the highest true rate the data still allows, at 95% confidence. With zero false you need about 190 sure sniffs before the bound drops under 2%.
That is why the ticket says: with too few pairs, wait a week rather than lower the bar.
sections.because: We gate on the upper bound, because a small sample's plain rate says more about luck than about the sniff.

notes.text: Inputs: how many were wrong, out of how many. z = 1.96 is the usual number for 95% confidence.
With no data the bound is 100%, so the go-live check fails closed.
The plain rate, for example 1 wrong in 300 is 0.0033.
The centre moves up a little for small samples, which is the Wilson correction.
The spread shrinks as n grows: more pairs, a tighter bound.
The top of the range. Compare this, not the plain rate, with the 2% bar.

p: When both bars hold on live data, the change is one key in Byte's config/repositories.json: fcp's sniff.observe becomes false. Every other key stays. Byte reviews the PR and Nave approves it.

Nothing else changes. A push that touches a sensitive path still gets a full review: SENSITIVE_PATH in Byte covers auth, migrations, workflows and infra. Any open high-severity finding still gets one, and @byte-review still forces one.

The sniff stays on Jev, not Haiku 5.5. A sniff costs about $0.0001: Jev is $0.042 per million input tokens against Haiku's $0.10. Its thresholds are tuned to jev-1.13.0 over four campaign runs. Watch the weekly harvest's re-flag rate for 2 weeks; above 2%, set observe back to true.
sections.because: We change one key in a reviewed policy file, so going live and going back are both a one-line PR.

quiz.q: Omer reviews Dana's PR, comments @byte-fix, Dana merges the fix, and Omer approves. What does the check on main do?

options.text: Passes: Omer is not the PR author, so his approval is independent
options.why: Since G2-05, the fix commit's trailer puts Omer in the requester set.

options.text: Fails: Omer is named in the fix commit's Requested-by trailer, so someone else must approve
options.why: He asked for code that is now in the PR; the requester never approves it.

options.text: Passes, because no CI ran on the fix PR
options.why: Fix PRs have no CI by design. The required checks run on main's PR after the merge, and the approval rule still applies.

quiz.q: fcp's observe-mode data shows 60 sure 'fulfilled' sniffs and none of them wrong. Can the sniff go live?

options.text: Yes: 0 of 60 is 0%, under the 2% bar
options.why: The plain rate ignores sample size. The Wilson upper bound for 0 of 60 is about 6%.

options.text: No: the Wilson upper bound is about 6%, so wait a week for more pairs
options.why: With zero wrong you need about 190 sure sniffs before the bound drops under 2%.

options.text: Yes, if we lower the bar to 6% for the first month
options.why: The ticket says to wait rather than lower the bar.

quiz.q: After G2-07 goes live, a push touches cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/migrations/ and the sniff says every finding is fixed and sure. What happens?

options.text: A full review still runs, because migrations are a sensitive path
options.why: SENSITIVE_PATH pushes, open high findings and @byte-review all still get a full review.

options.text: Only the short sniff line is posted
options.why: That is the live path for ordinary pushes; sensitive paths always get a full review.

options.text: Byte runs fix mode on the migration
options.why: Fix mode runs only when someone asks with @byte-fix.

words.plain: Byte's @byte-fix flow: plan, act, offline checks, then a PR into the author's branch, never into main.
A Key: value line at the end of a commit message that git can read back by key.
A known risk Security accepted for Byte, numbered in SECURITY.md, such as residual 1 or 3.
Byte's cheap per-push check on Jev: is each open finding fulfilled by this push, and how sure?
The sniff runs and records its verdict, but the full review runs too, so every verdict can be checked.
A sure 'fulfilled' sniff whose paired full review flagged the finding again.
The highest true rate a sample still allows at 95% confidence; small samples give a high bound.
